tools.description:
Execute a `bash` command. Use this for shell semantics — pipes, env, processes, git, package managers, build/test runners, anything genuinely interactive or multi-step.

**Translate these to a dedicated tool instead:**
- `cat` / `head` / `tail` (known path) → `Read`
- `sed` / `awk` (in-place edit) → `Edit`
- `echo > file` / `cat <<EOF` → `Write`
- `find` / recursive `ls` to locate files by name pattern → `Glob` (plain `ls <known-directory>` is fine for listing a directory)
- `grep` / `rg` (search file contents) → `Grep`
- `echo` / `printf` (talk to the user) → just output text directly

The dedicated tools render in the per-tool permission UI and keep raw stdout out of the conversation; that is why they are worth reaching for whenever one fits.

**Output:**
The stdout and stderr will be combined and returned as a string. The output may be truncated if it is too long. If the command exits non-zero, the output ends with a `Command failed with exit code: N` line; a command killed by its timeout or interrupted by the user ends with its own message instead.

Background execution is disabled for this agent. Do not set `run_in_background=true`.

**Guidelines for safety and security:**
- Each shell tool call will be executed in a fresh shell environment. The shell variables, current working directory changes, and the shell history is not preserved between calls. To run a command in a particular directory, pass the `cwd` argument (or use absolute paths) rather than relying on a `cd` from an earlier call.
- The tool call will return after the command is finished. You shall not use this tool to execute an interactive command or a command that may run forever. For possibly long-running commands, set the `timeout` argument in seconds. The default is 60s; foreground commands allow up to 300s; a foreground command that hits its timeout is killed.
- Avoid using `..` to access files or directories outside of the working directory.
- Avoid modifying files outside of the working directory unless explicitly instructed to do so.
- Never run commands that require superuser privileges unless explicitly instructed to do so.

**Guidelines for efficiency:**
- Use `&&` to chain commands that genuinely depend on each other, e.g. `npm install && npm test`. Independent read-only commands (separate `git show`, `ls`, or status checks) should be issued as separate parallel Bash calls in one response, not chained into a single call — chaining serializes their execution and mixes their output. Do not stitch outputs together with `echo` separators.
- Use `;` to run commands sequentially regardless of success/failure
- Use `||` for conditional execution (run second command only if first fails)
- Use pipe operations (`|`) and redirections (`>`, `>>`) to chain input and output between commands
- Always quote file paths containing spaces with double quotes (e.g., cd "/path with spaces/")
- Compose multi-step logic in a single call with `if` / `case` / `for` / `while` control flows.
- Do not set `run_in_background=true`; background task management tools are not available.

**Commands available:**
The following common command categories are usually available. Availability still depends on the host, so when in doubt run `which <command>` first to confirm a command exists before relying on it.
- Navigation and inspection: `ls`, `pwd`, `cd`, `stat`, `file`, `du`, `df`, `tree`
- File and directory management: `cp`, `mv`, `rm`, `mkdir`, `touch`, `ln`, `chmod`, `chown`
- Text and data processing: `wc`, `sort`, `uniq`, `cut`, `tr`, `diff`, `xargs`
- Archives and compression: `tar`, `gzip`, `gunzip`, `zip`, `unzip`
- Networking and transfer: `curl`, `wget`, `ping`, `ssh`, `scp`
- Version control: `git`; for GitHub-hosted work (PRs, issues, CI runs, API queries) prefer the `gh` CLI when installed — it carries the user's GitHub auth and can return structured JSON
- Process and system: `ps`, `kill`, `top`, `env`, `date`, `uname`, `whoami`
- Language and package toolchains: `node`, `npm`, `pnpm`, `yarn`, `python`, `pip` (use whichever the project actually relies on)

tools.name: Glob
tools.description:
Find files by glob pattern, sorted by modification time (most recent first).

Powered by ripgrep. Respects `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` by default — set `include_ignored` to also match ignored files (e.g. build outputs, `node_modules`). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) are always filtered out. Matches are files only — directories themselves are never listed; to find a directory, glob for a file inside it (e.g. `**/fixtures/**`).

Good patterns:
- `*.ts` — all files matching an extension, at any depth below the search root (a bare pattern without `/` matches recursively)
- `src/*.ts` — files directly inside `src/` (one level, not recursive)
- `src/**/*.ts` — recursive walk with a subdirectory anchor and extension
- `**/*.py` — recursive walk from the search root for an extension
- `*.{ts,tsx}` — brace expansion is supported
- `{src,test}/**/*.ts` — cartesian brace expansion is supported too

Results are capped at the first 100 matching paths. If a search would return more, a truncation marker is appended. Refine the pattern (extension, subdirectory) when 100 is not enough, or call again with a narrower anchor.

Large-directory caveat — avoid recursing into dependency / build output even with an anchor, especially when `include_ignored` is set:
- `node_modules/**/*.js`, `.venv/**/*.py`, `__pycache__/**`, `target/**` can produce thousands of results that truncate at the match cap and waste context. Prefer specific subpaths like `node_modules/react/src/**/*.js`.

path.description: Directory to search. Accepts an absolute path, or a path relative to the current working directory. Defaults to the current working directory.

include_ignored.description: Also match files excluded by ignore files such as `.gitignore`, `.ignore`, and `.rgignore` (for example `node_modules` or build outputs). Sensitive files (such as `.env`) remain filtered out for safety. VCS metadata directories (`.git` and similar) are always skipped, even when this is true. Defaults to false.

include_dirs.description: Deprecated and ignored. Results are always files-only — directories are never listed. Accepted only so older calls that still pass this flag are not rejected by parameter validation.

tools.description:
Search file contents using regular expressions (powered by ripgrep).

Use Grep when the task is to find unknown content or unknown file locations. Do not use shell `grep` or `rg` directly; this tool applies workspace path policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
ALWAYS use Grep tool instead of running `grep` or `rg` from a shell — direct shell calls bypass workspace policy, output limits, and sensitive-file filtering.
If you already know a concrete file path and need to inspect its contents, use Read directly instead.

Write patterns in ripgrep regex syntax, which differs from POSIX `grep` syntax. For example, braces are special, so escape them as `\{` to match a literal `{`.

Hidden files (dotfiles such as `.gitlab-ci.yml` or `.eslintrc.json`) are searched by default. To also search files excluded by `.gitignore` (such as `node_modules` or build outputs), set `include_ignored` to `true`. cat > /workspace/notes/06-quantize.md <<'EOF'
# Topic 06 — Quantization (`quantize`) — behavioral notes

Binary: `/workspace/executable` (fastText-like). All runs from `/tmp/probe-quant`.
Training data: 600-line, 3-class corpus (`train.txt`), 60-line `valid.txt` (both generated with `random.seed(42)`).

Models used:
- `supb.bin` — `supervised -input train.txt -output supb -thread 12 -dim 8 -minn 2 -maxn 5 -bucket 512` (46 words + 3 labels; input matrix 558×8; 18868 bytes)
- `sup.bin` — same but no subwords (input matrix 46×8; 2484 bytes)
- `sg.bin` — `skipgram -input train.txt -output sg -thread 1 -dim 8 -minCount 1 -minn 2 -maxn 5` (input matrix 2000046×8; 64003860 bytes)
- `ml.bin` — 300-label corpus `many.txt`, `supervised -dim 8 -thread 12 -epoch 3` (input 1793×8, output 300×8)

## 1. Basic `quantize -output X`

- Loads `<output>.bin` (NOT `-input`); writes `<output>.ftz`; **never modifies or re-saves the `.bin`** (md5 identical before/after).
- **Produces zero console output on success** (stdout and stderr both empty), at any `-verbose` level (tested 0, 1, 2). Exit code 0.
- Overwrites an existing `.ftz` silently.
- `-input` is not even opened unless `-retrain` is used: `quantize -input nosuch.txt -output supb` succeeds silently (exit 0).
- The input matrix must have **≥ 256 rows** or the process aborts:
  ```
  terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::invalid_argument'
    what():  Matrix too small for quantization, must have at least 256 rows
  ```
  (stderr, exit **134** = SIGABRT; no `.ftz` written, pre-existing `.ftz` left untouched).
  Triggered by: `sup.bin` (46 rows), and by any `-cutoff` < 256 (pruned matrix too small).
  Boundary verified: 255 rows → abort; 256 rows → OK.
- Fully deterministic: three identical runs give identical `.ftz` md5 (k-means seeded deterministically).

## 2. `.ftz` file format vs `.bin`

Identical 4-byte magic `ba 16 4f 2f` (0x2f4f16ba = 793712314) and version `0c 00 00 00` (12) for both.
Args section (12×int32: dim, ws, epoch, minCount, neg, wordNgrams, loss, model, bucket, minn, maxn, lrUpdateRate + double t) and dictionary section are **byte-identical** between `.bin` and `.ftz` (first diff at the quant flag, offset 882 in `supb`).

Dictionary: `size i32, nwords i32, nlabels i32, ntokens i64, pruneidx_size i64`, then per entry `word\0 count:i64 type:u8`. If pruned (cutoff), `pruneidx_size > 0` and `pruneidx_size` pairs of `(oldId:i32, newId:i32)` follow the words.

After the dictionary:
- `.bin`: `quant flag u8 = 0`, then dense input matrix `rows i64, cols i64, rows*cols f32`, then `qout flag u8 = 0`, then dense output matrix same layout.
- `.ftz`: `quant flag u8 = 1`, then a **QuantMatrix** for the input, then `qout flag u8`, then either a dense output matrix (qout=0) or a second QuantMatrix (qout=1).

QuantMatrix layout (verified byte-exact for several files):
```
qnorm      u8
m          i64        # rows
n          i64        # cols (= dim)
codesSize  i32        # = m * nsubq   (NOTE: int32 byte count, no dsub here)
codes      u8[codesSize]
PQ header  4 x i32:   dim, nsubq, dsub, lastdsub
centroids  f32[256 * n]   # ksub=256, per-dim codebook
if qnorm:
  norm codes   u8[m]          # NO size prefix (asymmetric with codes above)
  norm PQ hdr  4 x i32: 1, 1, 1, 1
  norm centroids f32[256]
```
Size accounting checks out exactly (e.g. qnorm file: 883 + 1+8+8+4 + 2232 + 16 + 8192 + 558 + 16 + 1024 + 1 + 16 + 96 = 13055 = file size).
Note vs upstream fastText: this build stores an explicit `codesSize` int32 and a 4×i32 PQ header `(dim, nsubq, dsub, lastdsub)`; dsub is not stored as a separate int64.

With `-qout`, the output matrix uses the identical QuantMatrix layout (e.g. qout flag=1, then `qnorm u8, m=299, n=8, codesSize=1196, codes, PQ(8,4,2,2), centroids`). `-qnorm` applies to the output QuantMatrix too (both get qnorm=1).

## 3. Options

Flags are pure switches — they take NO value. `quantize ... -qnorm true` →
`Provided argument without a dash! Usage:` + full usage dump, exit 1.
(The usage dump prints *current* parsed values: after `-qnorm` was consumed the dump shows `-qnorm ... [true]` whereas a fresh dump shows `[false]`.)

- `-qnorm`: adds norm-codes (m bytes) + norm codebook (256 f32) with PQ header `(1,1,1,1)`. Also changes the main codes/centroids (vectors are normalized before quantization) — whole file differs from non-qnorm run.
- `-qout`: quantizes the output/classifier matrix. On the 3-label model it aborts with the same `Matrix too small for quantization, must have at least 256 rows` (exit 134). Works with 300 labels.
- `-dsub` (default 2):
  - `-dsub 3` with dim 8 (3 ∤ 8): **works**, exit 0. PQ header `(8, 3, 3, 2)` — lastdsub = 2.
  - `-dsub 4`: PQ header `(8, 2, 4, 4)`.
  - `-dsub 16` (> dim): **works**. codesSize = m*1, PQ header `(8, 1, 16, 8)` — dsub stored as given, nsubq=1, lastdsub=dim.
  - `-dsub 0`: **SIGFPE, exit 136, no message at all** (division by zero).
  - `-dsub -2`: `terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::length_error'` / `what():  vector::_M_default_append`, exit 134.
- `-cutoff N`: keeps N total rows (top words + top ngram buckets). Dictionary is pruned (labels always kept) and a `pruneidx` map `(oldId,newId)` i32 pairs is written (`pruneidx_size = N - keptWords`; e.g. cutoff 256 → 23 words + 3 labels kept, pruneidx_size 233, matrix 256 rows).
  - N > total rows (e.g. 100000 > 558): no-op — output `.ftz` **byte-identical** to no-cutoff (md5 `10c2eeb9...`).
  - N = 0 or negative (e.g. -5): treated as disabled, byte-identical to default.
  - 0 < N < 256: aborts "Matrix too small..." (pruned matrix below 256 rows).
- `-retrain` (only meaningful with `-cutoff`; without cutoff it is a silent no-op, output byte-identical to default):
  - Retrains embeddings after pruning. Prints ONLY a progress line to **stderr**, no `Read 0M words` line (unlike training). Exact bytes (via `| cat -A`):
    ```
    ^MProgress: 100.0% words/sec/thread:   40815 lr: -0.000012 avg.loss:  0.777867 ETA:   0h 0m 0s^MProgress: 100.0% words/sec/thread:   40748 lr:  0.000000 avg.loss:  0.777867 ETA:   0h 0m 0s$
    ```
    (Note the transient negative lr `-0.000012` and the >100% progress overshoot — same cosmetic quirk as training, which also prints e.g. `Progress: 100.3% ... lr: -0.000316`.)
  - `-epoch` / `-lr` are honored during retrain: `-epoch 10 -lr 0.5` → avg.loss 0.063276 vs 0.777867 with defaults (epoch 5, lr 0.05).

## 4. Quantizing a skipgram (unsupervised) model

Always aborts, regardless of extra flags (`-qout`, `-cutoff` make no difference):
```
terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::invalid_argument'
  what():  For now we only support quantization of supervised models
```
exit 134, no `.ftz` written. So quantization is supervised-only in this build.

## 5. Using the `.ftz`

`test`, `test-label`, `predict`, `predict-prob`, `nn`, `analogies`, `print-word-vectors`, `print-sentence-vectors`, `print-ngrams`, `dump` all accept the `.ftz` path directly. `analogies` prints `Loading model supb.ftz` then `Query triplet (A - B + C)? `.

- Predictions differ slightly from `.bin` (quantization error), e.g.:
  ```
  .bin: __label__sport 0.345966 __label__tech 0.328106
  .ftz: __label__sport 0.345964 __label__tech 0.328145
  ```
- `print-word-vectors` works, values close to but not equal to `.bin`.
- `test`/`test-label` output format identical to `.bin` runs.
- Pruned (cutoff) model still returns vectors for pruned-away words (subword fallback via pruneidx remap).
- `dump args` and `dump dict` work on `.ftz` (same format as `.bin`).
- `dump input` / `dump output` on `.ftz`: print `Not supported for quantized models.` to **stderr**, exit code **0** (no stdout).

### QUIRK: `print-ngrams` prints uninitialized garbage (also on plain `.bin`!)
`print-ngrams supb.bin team` (and `.ftz`) emits absurd values — `-nan`, `-9.4576e+23`, `1.9927e+08` — for *some* vector components while others are sane. **Non-deterministic**: two identical runs differ (md5 mismatch); garbage positions/values vary per line and per run (e.g. one run: `<t 6.0779e+35 0.068016 6.0779e+35 ...` where columns 0 and 2 share the same garbage). Looks like reading uninitialized memory in the ngram-vector buffer. Exit code 0 regardless. `print-word-vectors`, `nn`, `predict` are NOT affected.

## 6. Error cases summary

| Case | Behavior | Exit |
|---|---|---|
| missing `<output>.bin` | `terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::invalid_argument'` / `what():  nosuch.bin cannot be opened for loading!` | 134 |
| missing `-output` (or `-input` value empty) | `Empty input or output path.` + usage | 1 |
| bare `quantize` (no args) | full usage text | 1 |
| missing `-input` file, no `-retrain` | silently ignored, quantizes fine | 0 |
| **missing `-input` file WITH `-retrain -cutoff`** | **HANGS FOREVER** — no output, no file, killed by timeout (>60 s; also with `-thread 1`) | — |
| input matrix < 256 rows | `std::invalid_argument`: `Matrix too small for quantization, must have at least 256 rows` | 134 |
| `-qout` with < 256 labels | same "Matrix too small" abort (output matrix) | 134 |
| quantize skipgram/cbow model | `std::invalid_argument`: `For now we only support quantization of supervised models` | 134 |
| `-dsub 0` | SIGFPE, no message | 136 |
| `-dsub < 0` | `std::length_error`: `vector::_M_default_append` | 134 |
| quantize an already-quantized file (`cp X.ftz Y.bin; quantize -output Y`) | **SIGSEGV, no message** | 139 |
| flag given a value (`-qnorm true`) | `Provided argument without a dash! Usage:` + usage | 1 |

All `terminate called ...` messages go to stderr (two lines, each `\n`-terminated).

## 7. Other observations

- Quantize success is 100% silent — the only way to confirm is the `.ftz` file appearing.
- Deterministic for fixed args/model (identical md5 across runs), including `-cutoff`.
- `.ftz` is smaller than `.bin` here mostly because dense f32 rows (32 B/row at dim 8) become 4 code bytes/row + one shared 8 KB codebook (e.g. 18868 → 11457 bytes).
- The supervised training run itself prints the >100% progress / negative-lr cosmetic quirk (`Progress: 101.0% ... lr: -0.000977` then a corrected final `Progress: 100.0% ... lr:  0.000000`), also seen in quantize-retrain output.
